I build and test expected-return models on large U.S. stock-characteristic panels, and the tools that take a model to a portfolio and make that step checkable. My research (PhD in Finance, Imperial College London, 2026) studies regularised and latent-factor estimators on 36 to 153 characteristics built from CRSP/Compustat; I work in Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn) and MATLAB. Outside the papers, I helped build the Python research platform of the Imperial Student Investment Fund, which works as a student finance lab. Each page states what I built, what the evidence shows and where it stops.

### [Return-State Behavior Profile](/projects/return-state-diagnostics.html)
[Portfolio behaviour and risk diagnostics]{.pcard-sub}

How did a return stream behave in normal months, strong rallies, recoveries, downturns and tail months? From dated strategy and benchmark returns, the function computes conditional returns, downside beta and hit frequencies for each market state, with observation counts and small-sample warnings.

::: {.pcard-details}
- **Example data:** an archived long–short U.S. equity backtest from my own research, monthly data Apr 2007 – Nov 2025 (224 months); a research case study, not an audited track record, and a configuration selected from several in an earlier study (selection bias not corrected); its signal loadings were estimated on a sample that may overlap the backtest period, so it is not an out-of-sample result.
- **Interactive demonstration:** 7 return streams (four archived, three built from public market and Treasury-bill returns) × 3 state definitions on the full sample, 21 results computed at build time. Half-sample results are not published, because they would let single months of the unpublished stream be reconstructed.
- **Not claimed:** future returns, actual trading, or a factor swap on fixed data; a new factor needs a new backtest before these diagnostics apply.
:::

[[risk diagnostics]{.chip} [market-state analysis]{.chip} [downside beta]{.chip} [tail observation counts]{.chip}]{.pcard-chips}

[[**Explore risk diagnostics**](/projects/return-state-diagnostics.html#demo) · [Metric definitions](/projects/return-state-diagnostics.html#outputs)]{.pcard-links}

[[Implemented & tested: evaluation code]{.status-badge .sb-built} · macro forecast evaluation · example: [Archived research example]{.status-badge .sb-measured}]{.pcard-meta}

### [Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics](/projects/forecast-evaluation.html)
[Forecast evaluation workbench]{.pcard-sub}

How should competing forecasts be judged when economic relationships change? From per-origin forecast records, the function scores models on the same origins, horizon and target, tracks the cumulative loss differential and tests the null of equal predictive accuracy (Diebold–Mariano test), next to a monitor of inflation persistence.

::: {.pcard-details}
- **Example data:** UK services inflation, February 2026 research snapshot; ONS monthly data through Dec 2025.
- **Interactive demonstration:** output version, horizon, model and comparison window switch among results computed at build time from the archived records.
- **Not claimed:** a forecast, an operational forecasting service, or that one model forecasts better in general.
:::

[[expanding-window pseudo-out-of-sample evaluation, look-ahead documented]{.chip} [forecast benchmark design]{.chip} [information timing]{.chip} [robustness checks]{.chip}]{.pcard-chips}

::: {.terms}
**Terms used on these pages.** To say how much of a stock's expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is; the rule it uses is the ruler (formally, a metric: an inner product on combinations of characteristics). A combination (a direction) gives every stock a score; it is not a portfolio. The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone; the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric, taken from the characteristics' cross-sectional Gram matrix) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks. A ruler is a measurement convention, not a better model. IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis) is a latent-factor model whose loadings are linear in stock characteristics; NA-IPCA (No-Arbitrage IPCA) rebuilds it on the characteristic ruler and adds a capped intercept, the part of expected return no factor in the model explains.
:::

## Machine learning and portfolios {#machine-learning-and-portfolios}

[Factor-model forecasts, rolling U.S. backtests and controlled comparisons, followed to holdings, risk and costs.]{.projects-group-lead}

::: {.paper-cards}

::: {.pcard}
[[Measured]{.status-badge .sb-measured} · working paper, October 2026]{.pcard-meta}

### [Which positions a factor model represents: exposures, hedges and holdings](/research/the-ruler-matters.html)

Expanding an IPCA library from 36 to 153 U.S. stock characteristics raises in-sample fit, yet the model's factors represent momentum and size positions less fully. Measured on the stocks actually held, a hedge built with the plain ruler leaves 46.10% of a value position, by squared stock weight, still lined up with the model's factor loadings (pp. 4–6). A check to run before trusting a better-fitting model for hedging.

::: {.pcard-details}
- 225 monthly formation dates, March 2007 to November 2025; models re-estimated each March on the previous 240 months, 19 times (Section II.A, p. 9; Table I, p. 10).
- Three latent factors plus six observed ones (market, size, value, profitability, investment and momentum), with and without a characteristic intercept, on 36 and 153 Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen characteristics in 11 economic groups (Section II.B, p. 11; Table I, p. 10).
- Stocks split permanently into disjoint source and target groups by a fixed hash: the factors are learned on one group and evaluated on the other (p. 9).
- Hedging rules compared at the same characteristic target: the plain-ruler (coefficient) hedge, the loading-neutral hedge measured on current stocks, and a historical minimum-variance hedge (Section V, pp. 24–25).
- Gross holdings, one-way turnover and subsequent variance for every policy, with simultaneous intervals over families of twelve comparisons from a twelve-month block bootstrap (Section II.C, pp. 12–15); turnover measures trading volume, not costs (p. 13).
:::

[[factor models (IPCA)]{.chip} [hedging and exposure control]{.chip} [block-bootstrap inference]{.chip} [holdings and turnover accounting]{.chip}]{.pcard-chips}

### [Building the characteristic ruler](/projects/building-the-ruler.html)
[Stabilising a 153 × 153 matrix in rolling windows]{.pcard-sub}

Seven ways to estimate the 153 × 153 Gram matrix of the characteristics (the characteristic ruler), scored on how they split the fit and on numerical conditioning: the stability problem any researcher meets with a large rolling covariance matrix.

### [Universes, trading costs and backtest checks](/projects/strategy-notes.html) `<span id="strategy-notes-stock-size-universes-and-trading-costs" class="legacy-anchor"></span>`{=html}

Where the models' advantage holds across five stock-size universes; the one-way trading cost at which each model's average return falls to zero under a turnover proxy (87 to 146 bp; a sensitivity check, not a break-even cost); and a checklist of what each backtest number has and still lacks.

### [Same fit, different attribution](/projects/why-the-ruler-matters.html)
[A hidden ruler in statistical factor models]{.pcard-sub}

Same data, same fit, different attribution: switching the ruler (the metric) moves expected return between the factors and the intercept without changing how well the model fits.

### [NA-IPCA toolkit: estimation code with an audit trail](/projects/naipca-toolkit.html)

Two Python packages I wrote for IPCA-family factor models: one builds and checks the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric), the other fits the models and writes an audit record for every fit. The 618 rolling windows of the intercept fit in Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios were estimated with this release.
